fields.meta_title: What Is Repentance? A Biblical Definition
fields.description: Repentance is not grovelling but a turning — a change of mind that turns the whole life back to God. Here is what Scripture means by it, and why it is good news.
fields.body_html:
Repentance is one of the first words of the gospel and one of the most misheard. To many ears it sounds like grovelling — a religion of guilt, of endless self-punishment, of never feeling good enough. But biblical repentance is nothing so bleak. It is a turning: a change of mind that becomes a change of direction, as a person stops walking away from God and turns to walk toward him. Far from being bad news, it is the doorway into everything good, for it is the road home. When Jesus began to preach, this was his very first summons: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15).

What, then, is repentance? Not merely feeling sorry, and not merely trying harder, but something deeper and more freeing than either. Here is what Scripture means by it, and why it is such good news.

Repentance is a change of mind that turns the whole life

The word behind “repent” means to change one’s mind — but in the Bible it is never a merely mental event. It is a reorientation of the entire person. Peter put the two halves together: “Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3:19). First the inward change of mind, then the outward turning of the life. Paul described his whole ministry as calling people “that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance” (Acts 26:20).

So repentance is not finished when we feel remorse; it is finished when we turn. The prophets pictured it as leaving one road for another: “Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the Lord, that he may have compassion on him” (Isaiah 55:7). To forsake and to return — that is the shape of it. A sorrow that changes nothing is not yet repentance; a turning that leaves the old way behind is.

It is godly sorrow, not mere regret

Not all sorrow is repentance. There is a grief that heals and a grief that only crushes, and Paul distinguished them carefully: “godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). Worldly grief is sorry about consequences — being caught, being shamed, being made to suffer. Godly grief is sorry about the sin itself, because it is against God. The difference is everything. Judas felt remorse and hanged himself; Peter wept bitterly and was restored. Both had failed their Lord grievously, but one grief ran toward death and the other ran toward God. The tears look alike from the outside; it is their direction that reveals which is which.

David, after his great fall, prayed the classic prayer of godly sorrow: “Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight... Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:4, 10). He did not merely regret the mess; he grieved the offence to God and longed to be made new. That is the sorrow the Spirit works — not a despairing self-hatred, but a broken-hearted honesty that runs toward God rather than away from him.

Repentance is coming home

The most beautiful picture Jesus ever gave of repentance is the prodigal son. Notice how the story turns. In a far country, having wasted everything, the young man “came to himself” and said, “I will arise and go to my father” (Luke 15:17–18). That is repentance in a sentence: coming to yourself, and going to your Father. He rehearsed a confession, rose, and turned for home — and the astonishing thing is what met him there. “While he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him” (Luke 15:20).

Notice, too, what the father does not do. He does not lecture, does not extract a probationary period, does not make the son earn his way back to sonship. He interrupts the rehearsed confession with a robe, a ring, and a feast. That is the God to whom repentance turns — not one who receives us grudgingly on the far edge of his estate, but one who restores us fully and gladly to the family. Repentance believes this about God, and so it dares to come.

This is the truth that transforms repentance from dread into hope. The one we turn to is not a reluctant judge but a running Father. Repentance is not crawling back to a God who must be persuaded to take us; it is turning to a God who has been watching the road, longing for our return, ready to run. That is why heaven’s response to a single repentant sinner is not solemnity but celebration: “there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:10).

It is God’s kindness that leads us to it

We often imagine repentance as something we must work up in ourselves to appease an angry God. Scripture reverses the picture. It is God’s kindness that draws repentance out of us in the first place: “God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance” (Romans 2:4). And repentance itself is his gift, not merely our achievement — the early church marvelled that “God has granted repentance that leads to life” (Acts 11:18).

This means we do not have to manufacture the perfect frame of heart before we come. We ask God for it. If your heart feels hard and your sorrow shallow, the answer is not to despair but to pray, “Lord, grant me repentance; give me a heart that grieves what grieves you and turns to what you love.” The very desire to repent is already grace at work, the first tug of the Father drawing a wanderer home.

Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning

Repentance never travels alone. It is the negative half of a single movement whose positive half is faith — turning from sin and turning to Christ, like a coin with two faces. This is why Jesus joined them in his first sermon: “repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15). Paul summarized his entire message the same way, testifying “of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 20:21). You cannot truly turn away from sin without turning toward Someone; and you cannot truly turn to Christ without turning from what he died to save you from.

This guards us against two errors. The first is a “repentance” that is all grief and no gospel — endless self-flagellation that never lifts its eyes to the Saviour, which is not repentance but despair. The second is a “faith” that wants forgiveness but not change, that would take Christ as rescuer while keeping sin as king. Real conversion refuses both. It grieves sin and grasps Christ, forsakes the far country and runs to the Father. The two belong together, and where the Spirit works, they always come together.

Repentance is not a one-time act but a way of life

Repentance opens the Christian life, but it does not close behind us. The whole of the Christian walk is, in a sense, a life of ongoing turning — a daily returning to God as we discover fresh corners of the heart that need his light. This is not morbid; it is health. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). The Christian keeps short accounts with God, turning quickly rather than letting sin harden into a settled direction.

Nor is this turning a burden that steals joy. Quite the opposite — unconfessed sin is what steals joy, and repentance restores it. That is why the same David who prayed for a clean heart also prayed, “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (Psalm 51:12). The road of repentance always runs toward gladness, because it always runs toward God.

How to turn today

So how does a person actually repent? Not with a formula, but with an honest heart. Name the sin plainly to God rather than excusing it. Agree with him about it. Turn from it deliberately, and where you can, put right what you have wronged. Then trust the promise: the debt is blotted out, the welcome is sure, the Father is already running.

Jesus warned that repentance is not optional — “unless you repent, you will all likewise perish” (Luke 13:3) — precisely because the alternative is to keep walking away from the only source of life. But the warning is set inside an invitation, and the invitation is open now. You need not clean yourself up first; the turning itself is the coming home. Wherever you have wandered, however long, the road back is short, and there is Someone at the end of it who has been waiting for you all along. Arise, and go to your Father.
